“Good morning, America, and if you don’t know it yet, we’ve got a new President. Charlie, did anyone this time last year think that Fred Thompson could possibly be here now?”

The TV is turned on to Good Morning America, and you are rubbing the sleep from your weary eyes as you watch from your campaign HQ. You stayed up as late as you could, but the race was simply too close to call. All of the major networks had declared the race a toss up well into the wee hours of the night, and at last, you had no choice but to give in to a fitful night of sleep, uncertain of your electoral fate.

Early next morning, you were woken up by the ringing of a phone, Jeri’s eager voice on the other end of the line. She had already spoken to the press, already received the news: you had won. The moment is surreal. It’s one you had desperately hoped for, but to actually hear the words was like a revelation from above.

Now, you are watching Good Morning America, as hosts Diane Sawyer and Charlie Gibson discuss the fallout of the closest presidential election since the 19th century. As they do, your eyes fall on the map graphic they have displayed. Your states are colored bright red, Richards’ are blue. The margins could not have been tighter, but it doesn’t matter, you have achieved what you set out to do last year when you, then a no-name backbencher, announced your presidential campaign. You faced fierce opposition in the primaries, then from Vice-President Richards, but through it all, you never lost faith in yourself or your mission to restore traditional values to this country.

As Charlie and Diane move on to talking to some of the voters, you get a call from Richards, congratulating you on the result. You can tell she is personally hurting, and you can sympathize, so you accept her words graciously. And you reflect on exactly what this means for you, Jeri, and all the people who have supported you. After two landslide defeats, you have shown the Republican Party how to win again. You’ve proven that your blend of an unorthodox background and traditional conservative values are a winning formula, even if some doubters might claim you nearly let a winnable election slip away.

Now, it’s time to start planning for your presidency, and you can expect a rocky road early on, as your narrow margin of victory will leave many feeling either aggrieved or dissatisfied, so you will have to work hard to get your agenda passed. Making things more complicated still is the situation in Congress, where despite Republicans holding onto the House, Democrats have retained the Senate thanks to Jim Jeffords’ party switch, so you will have to find a way to make this fractured government function for at least the next two years.

Still, Reagan led the country into prosperity with a divided Congress, so perhaps you can do the same, and truly live up to your promise to be a unifying leader. If you can do that, you could certainly be re-elected in four years’ time, despite your tenuous standing as of this morning.

As for the Democrats, it is uncertain exactly who they will turn to now that Richards’ political career is almost certainly over. You may find yourself facing her running mate, John Kerry, or perhaps Wellstone will give it another go. You yourself may face a potential revolt given your incredibly slim victory, so be careful you don’t make too many enemies within the party, But all of that is still a long way off. You’ve got more important things to worry about, Mr. President-Elect, such as getting out there and giving your expectant supporters a victory address. Knowing Jeri, she’s already got it all set up. The rest, sir, is up to you.

“It has been a long, tense night for both campaigns, but we can now project that Fred Thompson has crossed 270 electoral votes…”

Tom Brokaw’s announcement late in the night comes as a massive relief to you, Jeri, and all of your staffers who stayed up to watch the returns. To nobody’s shock, the election was a nail-biter, with the polls showing a dead heat for weeks, and that would be borne out in the final results, as seemingly every swing state was coming down to just a few thousand votes - if that.

When the primaries began, you were a rank outsider, dismissed by the experts as a political also-ran, but you never let that talk get to you. Even though you faced challenges in the primaries and faced off against another formidable opponent in Vice-President Richards, you rose to the challenge, and now look at you: Fred Dalton Thompson, soon-to-be 43rd president of the United States. Inevitably, some will say you got lucky, that your narrow margin was owed more to the natural effect of voters swinging to the party out of power, to to the biases against electing a female president. There may be some kernels of truth to that, but no one can take this away from you.

Richards will call to concede tomorrow, you are certain. She’s not the kind of person to do otherwise. As your staff celebrates and you share a hug with Jeri, you reflect on how far you’ve come. A decade ago, you were a relatively small time actor, on nobody’s radar to win political office, not even Reagan had such a sudden and dramatic rise. Now, it is time to look ahead to the challenges you will face as the first president elected in the new millennium.

Republicans were able to keep the House on the back of your victory, but the Senate remains in the hands of the Democrats, partly thanks to Jim Jeffords’ party switch. This means we can expect gridlock to reign for at least two more years in Washington. Hopefully, you can get enough Democrats to work with you in at least the first year. Potentially, you will attempt to pass a long-overdue tax cut, or seek to roll back wasteful government spending. Alternatively, if campaign finance reform and Global Warming are still on your agenda, you may seek to address these issues, which should build some goodwill across the aisle, but expect more mainline conservatives to bristle at the prospect. Either way, you have a tough road ahead, but if you play your cards right, you could be re-elected in four years’ time.

As for the Democrats, it is uncertain exactly who they will turn to now that Richards’ political career is almost certainly over. You may find yourself facing her running mate, John Kerry, or perhaps Wellstone will give it another go. You yourself may face a potential revolt given your narrow victory, so be careful you don’t make too many enemies within the party. But all of that is still a long way off. You’ve got more important things to worry about, Mr. President-Elect, such as planning your victory speech. Godspeed, sir.

\";\nthompsonWinLand = \"

“Fred Thompson: The Republican Carter”

(The following is an excerpt from the introduction of a book with the above title)

After a stunning landslide victory in the 2000 election, Fred Dalton Thompson entered the White House with the largest conservative mandate since Reagan. He was hailed by his supporters as bringing forth a new era of politics, a conservatism that returned to the Burkian traditional, constitutional values of old rather than the then en vogue firebrand politics of Newt Gingrich. During his campaign, Thompson presented himself as a figure beyond politics, almost a sort of Everyman. He had been an attorney once, and even a minor Hollywood actor.

Now, he was the man who was going to remake the American government as its founders intended. On election night 2000, we seemed to be standing at the doorstep of a new political era - then, like a house of cards, it all fell apart.

Less than a year into his presidency, the September 11th attacks would lead to war with Iraq, and despite early approval, the revelation that the Bushes had Thompson’s ear all along did irreparable damage to his image as a man devoid of modern politics. Furthermore, Thompson constantly found himself at odds with the Republican Congress, which prioritized a deeply unpopular attempt to repeal the NHRA over Thompson’s agenda of fighting corruption.

With the economy backsliding, Thompson’s ratings, which had peaked at over 70%, were now almost as low as Bush at his nadir in the early 90s. Suddenly, what seemed impossible once became a reality. Enter John Kerry, beaten running mate of four years prior, recipient of three purple hearts, reminding voters of CuomoCare, the Bridge Act, a time of peace, all the things that people were already getting nostalgic for, and as suddenly as Thompson’s star had risen, he crashed back to earth, a narrow electoral college defeat. A one term president.

And yet, there are still many who believe that Thompson was dealt a rotten hand. That if not for 9/11, he could have become a transformative president in the style of Reagan and FDR. To this day, there remains a sharp divide in opinion amongst the GOP. Some see him as an ignored prophet, others as ultimately a lightweight with no substance, a Republican Carter. This sharp divide remains one of the lasting legacies of the enigmatic 43rd president…”

“You know something, Diane, as I’m looking at the map, I’m just in awe at how close this election was. I mean we’re talking - relatively speaking - a handful of votes here!”

The TV in your HQ is turned on to Good Morning America. You watch through exhausted eyes as they discuss the result of last night’s election while an electoral college map is displayed behind them. Your states are red, Richards’ are blue. Already that map is burned into your mind. You had known before you even turned on the television that your dreams of victory had been dashed.

You were woken up by a call from Jeri, who broke the news to you, the race had been called - but not in your favor, and already, she was out there fending off the press. As devastated as you were, there was some comfort in receiving the news from Jeri first. Your most trusted confidante, and maybe the person you will spend the rest of your life with. She is one of the few comforts you have right now.

Now, as you watch hosts Charlie Gibson and Diane Sawyer discuss the results of the election, the implications and what it means, you are wracked by what ifs. What if you had pushed a particular message more, what if you had spared just one more visit to a critical swing state? Was there anything more you could have said or done? Any times when you should have kept your mouth shut?

The doubts pierce you so deeply because you truly believed in this campaign, you believed so strongly in your vision for a traditional conservative America, one that puts the people first, but something about your message just didn’t land. You have come a long way from the nobody who first announced his presidential campaign to little fanfare. You had to overcome an intense challenge in the primaries, then faced an even stiffer test from Vice-President Richards, but in the end, it was simply not meant to be.

As Diane and Charlie continue discussing the election and begin interviewing some voters, you know what you need to do. You pick up the phone and make the call no politician ever wants to make: a concession call, but it’s the right thing to do. You can barely hide your disappointment, but Richards is understanding and accepts your words with grace. She will go on to become the first-ever female president, and hopefully embrace moderate positions rather than following in Cuomo’s footsteps. The good news for Republicans is that they have held on to the House, but the Senate remains in Democratic hands, thanks partly to Jim Jeffords’ party switch. This means gridlock will likely reign for at least the next two years.

At this moment, however, you don’t particularly care to ponder such things. Your role in this story is over, you have given all you had to this race, but now it’s time to take a step back and evaluate your future, You are not too old to not make a comeback, perhaps running for your soon-to-be vacated Senate seat or Tennessee’s governorship, but it is very unlikely you will ever get another chance to run for the top job. Perhaps you will still play a role in the selection process, if you so choose. Or perhaps, you’ve simply had enough of politics and are ready to quit altogether.

That choice is entirely yours, and Jeri, of course, will be right there beside you. Perhaps the two of you will still find some personal joy in your lives despite this setback. Right now, though, get ready to give your last speech as a presidential candidate to your faithful supporters. Best of luck, Senator. The next chapter of your life awaits.

“For those who have stayed with us, we do have a major projection: Vice-President Richards has just secured a historic victory…”

The race was razor thin, so close that the words “toss up” had been ingrained in the American consciousness for weeks. The only thing the pollsters were sure of was that this was going to be a very long Election Night, and that was exactly the way it turned out. For hours, Brokaw, Russert and their colleagues talked about the importance of this election, the stakes, the battle for control over America’s narrative in the new millennium. You had just about given up finding out, then Brokaw made his announcement, shattering at long last your exhausted, forlorn hopes. You feel Jeri’s hand on your shoulder. She was the only one who stayed up with you. Now, she is there to comfort you in this difficult time.

After all the ads, all the campaign stops, all the rallies, all the money, the blood, sweat, and tears, everything you had done was all for nought. Your unlikely bid to become President had ended in gut wrenching fashion. When the primaries began, you were dismissed as a lightweight, yet you’d proved to have an unorthodox charisma. People saw something in you, the vision of a better America. In the general election, there was very little to choose between you and Richards, but no matter how much you pushed your message, hers just seemed to resonate a little bit more.

You will call Richards the next day to wish her well. It’s the right thing to do, and you’ve always been a gentleman, whatever else people can say about you. Now, though, it is time to reflect on your career. As you have vacated running for re-election to the Senate, it is uncertain if you will attempt to run again for your old seat, seek a different office, or simply accept an early retirement. Perhaps the Governorship of Tennessee could be an option, as Don Sundquist is term-limited from running in 2002. You remain popular in your home state, regardless of this result.

Meanwhile, with Richards becoming the first ever-female president, only time will tell how she leads the country. Republicans still hold the House, so at the very least, conservatives will have a bulwark against the Left’s agenda, and in all likelihood, political gridlock will be the status quo for at least the next two years. As for the next GOP nominee to oppose her in ‘04, you may still have a bit of clout in the selection process, given how close the race was. Your endorsement, while perhaps not decisive, may well be sought after.

For now, though, your time in Washington is done, and these are concerns for another day. You are free to choose exactly how you will continue to fight for the ideas that you hold dear. Jeri, of course, will be right there beside you, and perhaps the two of you will still find some personal joy in your lives despite this setback. Best of luck, Senator. The next chapter of your life awaits.

\";\nthompsonLossLand = \"

“GOP presidential candidate draws criticism for saying he considers himself Fred Thompson-esque”

(The following is an excerpt from an article written about Mike Lee during his 2024 presidential campaign)

Mike Lee’s long shot bid to primary President Larry Hogan took another hit in the eyes of many Republicans today when he compared himself to former presidential candidate Fred Thompson. In comments made on Fox News on Monday night, Lee said that he considers himself a “Thompson conservative”, and that he believes the Universal Healthcare Act of 2009 could have been prevented had Thompson’s proposal to repeal and replace its predecessor, the National Healthcare Reform Act (NHRA) been taken seriously at the time. Thompson, then a Senator from Tennessee, had surprised many in the GOP establishment by not only seeking the nomination against more highly touted names like Jeb Bush, but successfully winning it.

In the general election against then-Vice President Ann Richards, Thompson notoriously ran on slashing or outright repealing government programs, particularly Social Security and the NHRA. Experts also believe that his role in deregulation of the S&L industry played a role in his polling taking a nosedive. While energizing many conservatives, Thompson’s mix of controversial views resulted in a resounding defeat in November, ending his presidential aspirations for good.

Despite this setback, Thompson continued to be an advocate for strict constitutional conservatism, vocally decrying the country’s move to a single payer healthcare system and lamenting the perceived decline of individual liberty and responsibility in America. While the national party would gradually undergo a moderate shift in the 2010s (culminating in the election of President Hogan in 2020), Thompson worked the rest of his life to keep his brand of politics alive. Today, his legacy is carried on by men like Lee, who has also previously stated that he knows he cannot unseat President Hogan, but merely seeks to remind the Republican Party of what they are supposed to be.

bill passed both chambers relatively easily, much to the anger of conservatives, and you caught some flak along with the other GOP “sellouts”. Meanwhile, early polling shows the act is quite popular nationally." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 91002, "fields": { "answer": 81002, "candidate": 77, "answer_feedback": "The Bridge act passed without your vote, and made it through both chambers relatively easily, over furious conservative protests. Thankfully, the right is mostly blaming the moderate Republicans who voted for it and Trent Lott for his failed leadership. Your “nay” vote wins the hearts of the conservative base, but early polling indicates that the act is quite popular nationally." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 91003, "fields": { "answer": 81003, "candidate": 77, "answer_feedback": "The feeling amongst Republicans is optimistic after the midterms, so this is a safe response and one that will not concern or offend anyone. Let’s hope that this is just a preview of the 2000 election and we can finally see some common sense return to the executive branch." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 91004, "fields": { "answer": 81004, "candidate": 77, "answer_feedback": "”It may be best to keep yourself distanced a bit from the Gingrichite wing. While you have a reputation back home as being a charming and more traditional conservative, many of the House members have a noticeable hardline streak that doesn’t sit well with the establishment." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 91005, "fields": { "answer": 81005, "candidate": 77, "answer_feedback": "The Right is already dreaming of what Newt Gingrich could pass as Speaker of the House once he has a cooperative Senate and President. Already, there are plans being drawn up for a major tax cut and welfare reform. You won’t get a chance to vote on many of them, but at least the GOP is making its presence known." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 91006, "fields": { "answer": 81006, "candidate": 77, "answer_feedback": "It’s never a bad idea to remain vigilant and prepared for the next election. After all, those who rest on their laurels rarely prosper in politics. With any luck, you’ll be part of a Republican Senate majority come January of 2001." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 91007, "fields": { "answer": 81007, "candidate": 77, "answer_feedback": "It’s little more than lip service, but it’ll do the job of getting the press off your back. Gingrich's resignation has caught everyone in Washington off guard, and it is now anyone’s guess as to how the Republican House will operate in the next term." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 91008, "fields": { "answer": 81008, "candidate": 77, "answer_feedback": "A sentiment appreciated by moderates and used by Democrats to show that even fellow Republicans couldn’t stand Gingrich, but not one that’s going to do you any favors with the base, who still love Gingrich and have looked to him as their voice in Congress for years now." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 91009, "fields": { "answer": 81009, "candidate": 77, "answer_feedback": "If you’re going to comment on this fiasco, you’d do well to give the former Speaker some fan service to placate his supporters, and this response accomplishes just that. Let’s hope Hastert can be the unifying voice the GOP needs right now." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 91010, "fields": { "answer": 81010, "candidate": 77, "answer_feedback": "There’s probably not much good that can come out of wading into the political minefield that is the Gingrich resignation. Many of his former colleagues are toeing a similar line so you are far from alone in wanting to quickly move past this whole ordeal. Let’s hope Hastert can avoid making the same mistakes Gingrich made." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 91011, "fields": { "answer": 81011, "candidate": 77, "answer_feedback": "Impeachment is widely unpopular pretty much everywhere except the Deep South, so there is not much to lose by coming out forcefully against it, especially given that the evidence appears flimsy at best. In any event, Hastert is struggling to keep his members in line, and the impeachment eventually falls apart, to the detriment of the House GOP’s polling." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 91012, "fields": { "answer": 81012, "candidate": 77, "answer_feedback": "Impeachment is overwhelmingly unpopular with the electorate, so there is not much to lose by coming out against it here, which makes your slight hedge a bit interesting. Perhaps it was the right move if you want to avoid stepping on any toes. In the end, there does not appear to have been anything to all the impeachment talk." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 91013, "fields": { "answer": 81013, "candidate": 77, "answer_feedback": "Only the most partisan Republicans in the Deep South give the push for impeachment even a shred of credibility. Meanwhile, everyone else is wondering what the hell you’re talking about. “Tim, I think we have now to seriously consider the future of the Republican Party after Congressman Kasich leads them to yet another defeat. Where exactly do they go from here?”

You’re watching NBC’s election night coverage from your couch at home in Tennessee, watching as Tom Brokaw and Tim Russert break down the result, a historic victory for Vice President Ann Richards, as she is set to become the first-ever woman president. Truthfully, you’re not surprised Kasich lost. The man was a Gingrich acolyte and held some hardline positions that certainly hurt him with the electorate.

It didn’t have to be like this, you think to yourself. Republican voters had a choice, a choice to either embrace the zero sum game of the movement conservatives or take a chance on you, a relative outsider, a man presenting the party with a vision of true constitutional conservatism. Faced with that decision, the GOP had chosen self-immolation. You had followed the campaign from the convention to now; Kasich never even bothered trying to get your endorsement. You eventually offered a half-hearted one anyway, for the good of the party, but it mattered little in the end.

In the aftermath of this result, the GOP now faces a crisis of their own making. In 1996, the establishment chose a moderate, in 2000, the hard right got its way, and both had lost. Now the party is rudderless, directionless, unsure of where to turn next. After three consecutive defeats, it’s starting to feel like conservatives have simply forgotten how to win presidential elections. Of course, you tried to warn them of what would happen if they nominated Kasich. Perhaps now, they will listen. Perhaps, if you so wish, this will even give you the momentum to try for the nomination again in four years’ time.

Right now, however, another run is the last thing on your mind. As you sit there and continue watching the election coverage, you feel an overwhelming sense of melancholy and exhaustion. Your Senate term will expire in January, bringing an end to your time in Washington, for now at least. You hear the phone ringing, it’s probably Jeri, your partner, campaign manager, and closest confidante, calling to check in on you. She experienced all the highs and lows of the campaign alongside you, and will be your guiding light as you move into the next chapter of your life. Best of luck, Senator.
